claims.text: Formation of single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements under rapid thermal synthesis is governed by kinetic trapping.
An ultra-short nucleation dwell limits atomic interdiffusion.
Limited atomic or precursor mobility favors formation of a homogeneous random single phase.
The homogeneous single phase produced by rapid processing is metastable.
Extending the dwell at an intermediate temperature provides enough atomic mobility to cause segregation and phase separation.
The proposed initial state consists of uniformly dispersed mixed precursors for at least six noble-metal elements on an inert substrate or support, without a preformed phase.
The controlled intervention is to vary only the dwell time at an intermediate nucleation temperature during the thermal ramp.
Relevant rapid thermal synthesis can involve peak temperatures above 1100 K and millisecond-to-second heating and cooling cycles.
Dwell time modulates local ordering and atomic diffusion length scales.
Transient interdiffusion and early-stage crystalline-cluster nucleation mediate whether the material freezes into one phase or develops phase-separated regions.
Rapid heating combined with a short nucleation dwell suppresses atomic mobility.
Enhanced diffusion during a longer dwell drives local compositional fluctuations that produce elemental segregation and secondary phases.
Minimal-dwell samples will predominantly exhibit a single solid-solution phase with uniform elemental distribution.
Minimal-dwell samples will have controlled nanoparticle morphology.
Extended-dwell samples will exhibit more phase separation and elemental segregation than minimal-dwell samples.
Extended dwell may alter particle shapes or particle-size distributions through prolonged atomic mobility.
A rapid heating and cooling cycle without an intermediate dwell can yield a metastable single-phase HEA nanoparticle structure.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles with more than five elements in millisecond-to-second thermal regimes where diffusion remains limited.
The threshold dwell time separating kinetic trapping from diffusion-driven segregation is unknown.
A lack of any detectable increase in segregation, phase separation, or morphology change across extended dwell times is specified as the falsifying result.
